facts.statement: The genus Udanoceratops was described by Kurzanov in 1992.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Kurzanov, 1992

facts.statement: Udanoceratops is a large leptoceratopsid dinosaur that lived in Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops (meaning "Udan-Sayr horned face") is a genus of large leptoceratopsid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of Mongolia.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered in the 1980s during the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, the partial skeleton of an adult with its bones encapsulated in calcium carbonate, was discovered in the 1980s as part of the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition

facts.statement: Sergei Kurzanov described the genus in 1992.
facts.quote: In 1992, it was described by palaeontologist Sergei Kurzanov.

facts.statement: The only known species is Udanoceratops tschizhovi, named after D. O. Tschizhov.
facts.quote: The sole species of Udanoceratops, also the type species, is Udanoceratops tschizhovi, named after a colleague of Kurzanov, D. O. Tschizhov.

facts.statement: Some additional remains assigned to Udanoceratops may be misattributions.
facts.quote: Additional remains have been assigned to Udanoceratops, though these may be misattributions.

facts.statement: Udanoceratops is the largest known leptoceratopsid, estimated to be about 4 meters long and 700 kg in weight.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops is the largest known leptoceratopsid, with some estimates placing it at about 4 m in length and 700 kg in weight.

facts.statement: The skull was deeper and more robust than other leptoceratopsids, featuring larger nasal cavities and a heavier beak.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops' skull was far deeper and more robust than that of other leptoceratopsids, with larger nasal cavities and presumably a heavier beak.

facts.statement: Projections on the cheek bones likely supported a large patch of keratin.
facts.quote: The projections on Udanoceratops' cheek bones would have supported a large patch of keratin.

facts.statement: The snout bone above the beak was smooth, lacking horns or tubercles found in related taxa.
facts.quote: The bone of its snout above the beak was completely smooth, bearing neither the horns nor the slight tubercles of related taxa.

facts.statement: The teeth had a slicing mechanism similar to that of Archaeoceratops and Leptoceratops.
facts.quote: The lower teeth bore shelves into which the upper set would have slotted when the jaw was closed. This would have resulted in a slicing action, similar to the system present in Archaeoceratops and Leptoceratops.

facts.statement: The tail was very tall and compressed from side to side, similar to other leptoceratopsids and protoceratopsids.
facts.quote: Its tail was very tall and was somewhat compressed from side-to-side, as in many other leptoceratopsids and protoceratopsids.

facts.statement: While some suggest Udanoceratops was semi-aquatic, its claw shape is more likely an adaptation for walking on soft substrates like sand dunes.
facts.quote: This and the shape of its unguals (the bones which would have supported its claws) has led to suggestions that Udanoceratops was semi-aquatic, but it is more likely that the shape of its unguals was an adaptation to supporting its weight on soft substrate such as sand dunes.

facts.statement: Bipedal running is unlikely; if it ran, it likely did so on all fours and was slower than smaller relatives.
facts.quote: Similarly, while it has been suggested that Udanoceratops could have run bipedally, this appears to be unlikely. If it did run, it likely would have done so on all fours, and would have been significantly slower than its smaller relatives.

facts.statement: Fossils are known from the Djadochta Formation in Mongolia, an area also famous for Protoceratops and Velociraptor.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops is known from the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia, which is well known for the fossils of Protoceratops and Velociraptor which have been recovered there.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen PIN 3907/11 was collected in the 1980s by the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition.
facts.quote: The holotype (PIN 3907/11) of Udanoceratops was collected in the 1980s as part of the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition.

facts.statement: The holotype was found at the Udan-Sayr locality in dark grey sandstones designated as Bed 2.
facts.quote: It was recovered from the Udan-Sayr (also spelled Udyn Sayr or Üüden Sair) locality from a layer of dark grey sandstones designated as Bed 2.

facts.statement: The Udan-Sayr locality is part of the Djadochta Formation, dated to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The Udan-Sayr locality is part of the Djadochta Formation of Ömnögovi Province, which has been dated to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The holotype preserves a near-complete skull, several vertebrae, shoulder bones, hip bones, and some limb bones.
facts.quote: PIN 3907/11 preserves a near-complete skull, several vertebrae, a scapula, a coracoid, an ilium, and at least some bones from the extremities.

facts.statement: All bones were encapsulated in calcareous structures, either as concretions or a single mass.
facts.quote: All of its bones were encapsulated within calcareous structures, either within concretions or as part of a single, larger mass.

facts.statement: The specimen was moved to the Paleontological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences and cleaned with acetic acid.
facts.quote: The specimen was relocated to the Paleontological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences and was removed from the matrix through the use of acetic acid.

facts.statement: Sergei Kurzanov described the species as Udanoceratops tschizhovi in 1992.
facts.quote: In 1992, it was described by Russian palaeontologist Sergei Kurzanov, and was assigned the binomial name of Udanoceratops tschizhovi.

facts.statement: The genus name combines the locality name Udan-Sayr with Greek words for 'horn' and 'face', while the species name honors D. O. Tschizhov.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the name of the locality in which the holotype was found (Udan-Sayr) and Greek ceras/κέρας meaning "horn" and -ops/ωψ meaning "face"; the species name honours D. O. Tschizhov of the Paleontological Institute, who was credited with the discovery of the specimen.

facts.statement: It is debated whether a large skull from the Bayan Mandahu Formation belongs to Udanoceratops; some researchers suspect it was misidentified as Protoceratops hellenikorhinus.
facts.quote: In 1993 a large skull almost 1 m in length was reported from the nearby Bayan Mandahu Formation by Tomasz Jerzykiewicz and colleagues and was assigned to Udanoceratops. However, Polish palaeontologist Łukasz Czepiński in 2020 pointed out that there are no referable specimens to Udanoceratops from the Bayan Mandahu collections, and there are none in the literature which correspond to the reported remains. Therefore, he suspected that Jerzykiewicz and colleagues confused Udanoceratops with the contemporary (and relatively large) Protoceratops hellenikorhinus.

facts.statement: The status of a juvenile specimen (PIN 4046/11) is debated, with some studies considering it an indeterminate leptoceratopsid rather than Udanoceratops.
facts.quote: In 2004 Viktor S. Tereschenko referred a juvenile specimen (PIN 4046/11) to Udanoceratops aff. tschizhovi, from the Baga Tariach locality in Dornogovi Province, which Tereschhenko attributed to the Djadochta Formation. Geological analyses carried out across fossil-bearing localities of the Gobi Desert, published by Mahito Watabe and colleagues in 2010, indicates that this locality correlates best with the Maastrichtian-stage Barun Goyot Formation. The status of PIN 4046/11 has varied since then. It has been classified as "Udanoceratops" sp. and ?Udanoceratops sp, and some studies, including one authored by Tereschenko himself, consider it an indeterminate leptoceratopsid.

facts.statement: Estimates place the length at nearly 4 meters and the weight at about 700 kg.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops was a large ceratopsian, estimated by V. S. Tereschenko to have reached nearly 4 m in length, and by Gregory S. Paul to have weighed about 700 kg.

facts.statement: It is currently the largest named leptoceratopsid, though fragmentary remains from Kazakhstan might represent a similarly sized animal.
facts.quote: It is the largest named leptoceratopsid known so far, though fragmentary remains from Kazakhstan may belong to an animal of similar body size.

facts.statement: Kurzanov suggested in 1992 that Udanoceratops was two to three times the size of Protoceratops.
facts.quote: Writing about the genus in 1992, Kurzanov suggested that it may have been anywhere between two and three times the size of Protoceratops, to which he believed it was closely related.

facts.statement: The skull of Udanoceratops was significantly larger and taller than those of other leptoceratopsids and protoceratopsids.
facts.quote: The skull of Udanoceratops is considerably larger, both in general size and in height, than that of other leptoceratopsids and protoceratopsids.

facts.statement: Kurzanov reported that the skull of Udanoceratops measured 60 to 70 cm in length.
facts.quote: Kurzanov noted that its skull, which measured 60–70 cm in length, was roughly half as long again as that of the North American Montanoceratops

facts.statement: The dorsal portions of the nasal bones of Udanoceratops were smooth and lacked horns or tubercles.
facts.quote: Unlike many other ceratopsians, where either a full horn or a slight tubercule was present on the nasal bones, at least the dorsal (top) portions of Udanoceratops' nasals appear to have sported nothing at all, as the bone texture is completely smooth there.

facts.statement: Udanoceratops possessed an extremely deep lower jaw compared to related taxa.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops had an extremely deep mandible (lower jaw), considerably more so than that of related taxa.

facts.statement: Kurzanov suggested that Udanoceratops engaged in ritual head-swinging confrontations between two individuals, likely males.
facts.quote: Kurzanov forwarded the idea that Udanoceratops engaged in ritual confrontations wherein two individuals, presumably males, would inflict blows on one another by swinging their heads sideways and upwards

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul suggested in 2016 that a break on the holotype skull was caused by the beak of another individual rather than ritual combat.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul, in 2016, instead suggested that the break may have been inflicted by the beak of another individual.

facts.statement: Kurzanov suggested that the teeth of Udanoceratops functioned only as cutting mechanisms.
facts.quote: Kurzanov suggested, consequently, that Udanoceratops' teeth could operate "only as cutting mechanisms".

facts.statement: The number of teeth on the maxilla of Udanoceratops has been reported as either twelve or fifteen.
facts.quote: The number of teeth on the maxilla has variously been reported as either twelve, or fifteen.

facts.statement: The roots of the dentary teeth of Udanoceratops numbered either twelve or eighteen and were identical to those of the upper jaw.
facts.quote: The roots of the dentary teeth, of which there were either twelve, or eighteen, were identical to those on the upper jaw

facts.statement: V. S. Tereschenko noted in 2008 that Udanoceratops likely had nine cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: V. S. Tereschenko, in 2008, noted that (assuming PIN 4046/11 belongs to this genus) Udanoceratops had nine cervical (neck) vertebrae

facts.statement: Based on related taxa, Udanoceratops likely had nine thoracic, three lumbar, eight sacral, and between 38 and 50 caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: based on other leptoceratopsids and protoceratopsids, it likely had nine thoracic (upper torso), three lumbar (lower torso), eight sacral (within the sacrum), and somewhere between 38–50 caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: V. S. Tereschenko argued that bipedal locomotion in Udanoceratops was very unlikely and that the assumption of short forelimbs lacked sufficient foundation.
facts.quote: However, V. S. Tereschenko noted that this is very unlikely, and that Chinnery had assumed "without sufficient foundation" that Udanoceratops had proportionally short forelimbs.

facts.statement: Udanoceratops measured approximately 4 meters in length and 700 kilograms in weight, making it the largest known leptoceratopsid.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops medía aproximadamente 4 metros de largo y 700 kiilogramos de peso, siendo el leptoceratópsido más grande conocido hasta ahora.

facts.statement: The skull had a short frill and lacked horns above the eyes or on the nose.
facts.quote: El cráneo tenía un volante corto y no tenía cuernos sobre los ojos o la nariz.

facts.statement: The skull measured approximately 60 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: Su cráneo medía unos 60 centímetro de largo.

facts.statement: The lower jaw was distinctly robust.
facts.quote: La mandíbula inferior era distintivamente robusta.

facts.statement: It lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 83 to 71 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 83 y 71 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Asia.

facts.statement: It was first named and described by Russian paleontologist Sergei Kurzanov in 1992, with the type species being Udanoceratops tschizhovi.
facts.quote: Udanoceratops fue nombrado y descrito por primera vez por el paleontólogo ruso Sergei Kurzanov en 1992 y la especie tipo es Udanoceratops tschizhovi.

facts.statement: The holotype, PIN 3907/11, was collected in the 1980s from the Udan Sayr locality in the Djadokhta Formation of the Ömnögovi Province, dating to the Campanian stage of the Upper Cretaceous.
facts.quote: El holotipo, PIN 3907/11, se recolectó durante la década de 1980 en la localidad de Udan Sayr, también deletreado Udyn Sayr o Üüden Sair, de la Formación Djadokhta en la provincia de Ömnögovi, que data de la etapa Campaniense del período Cretácico superior.

facts.statement: The generic name is derived from the type locality Udan Sayr and the Greek words for "horn" and "face".
facts.quote: El nombre genérico se deriva del nombre de la localidad en la que se encontró el holotipo, Udan Sayr, y del griego ceras, κέρας que significa "cuerno" y -ops, ωψ que significa "cara".

facts.statement: It is placed within the Leptoceratopsidae, being the only Asian representative at the time alongside the North American Leptoceratops, Montanoceratops, and Prenoceratops.
facts.quote: Se ubica dentro de los Leptoceratopsidae, como único representante asiático en ese momento, junto con los norteamericanos Leptoceratops, Montanoceratops y Prenoceratops.

facts.statement: In 2008 and 2013, Tereschenko suggested that Udanoceratops had somewhat aquatic habits based on its high neural spines, laterally compressed tail, and ungual shape.
facts.quote: In 2008, Tereschenko suggested that Udanoceratops was somewhat aquatic in its habits, based on its high neural spines, the lateral compression of its tail, and the shape of its ungual (which he suggested also implied semiaquatic tendencies in Protoceratops); he argued the same in a paper published in 2013 co-authored with T. Singer.

facts.statement: In a subsequent paper, Tereschenko rejected the aquatic hypothesis, suggesting instead that the ungual shape correlated with supporting weight on loose substrate without sinking.
facts.quote: In a subsequent paper, however, he rejected this hypothesis, suggesting that the ungual shape of the genus instead correlated more to supporting the animal's weight on loose substrate without sinking.

facts.statement: In 1993, paleontologist Tomasz Jerzykiewicz reported a large skull, nearly 1 meter long, assigned to Udanoceratops from the nearby Bayan Mandahu Formation.
facts.quote: En 1993, el paleontólogo Tomasz Jerzykiewicz informó sobre un cráneo grande, "casi 1 m de largo", asignado a Udanoceratops en la cercana Formación Bayan Mandahu.

facts.statement: However, in 2020, paleontologist Łukasz Czepiński noted that there are no specimens attributable to Udanoceratops from the Bayan Mandahu collections, suggesting they were likely confused with the concurrent and relatively large Protoceratops hellenikorhinus.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, el paleontólogo polaco Łukasz Czepiński señaló en 2020 que no hay especímenes atribuibles a Udanoceratops de las colecciones de Bayan Mandahu, y lo más probable es que estos restos se hayan confundido con el concurrente y relativamente grande Protoceratops hellenikorhinus.

facts.statement: In 2004, Viktor S. Tereschhenko assigned a juvenile specimen, PIN 4046/11, from the Baga Tariach locality to Udanoceratops aff. tschizhovi, attributing it to the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: En 2004, Viktor S. Tereschhenko remitió un espécimen juvenil, PIN 4046/11 a Udanoceratops aff. tschizhovi, de la localidad de Baga Tariach en la provincia de Dornogovi, que Tereschhenko atribuyó a la Formación Djadokhta.

facts.statement: Geological analyses published by Mahito Watabe and his team in 2010 indicate that the Baga Tariach locality correlates better with the Barun Goyot Formation of the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: Los análisis geológicos llevados a cabo en las localidades fosilíferas del desierto de Gobi publicados por Mahito Watabe y su equipo en 2010 indican que esta localidad, en cambio, se correlaciona mejor con la formación Barun Goyot en etapa Maastrichtiense.
